claim: Slc35g3 comprises two coding exons and is located on chromosome 11 in mice.
source: In mice, Slc35g3 comprises two coding exons and is located on chromosome 11, whereas it is located on chromosome 17 in humans.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text about the gene structure and chromosomal location.

claim: Slc35g3 is located on chromosome 17 in humans.
source: In mice, Slc35g3 comprises two coding exons and is located on chromosome 11, whereas it is located on chromosome 17 in humans.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text about the chromosomal location in humans.

claim: Slc35g3 is evolutionarily conserved among vertebrates.
source: The TreeFam (Ruan et al., 2008) data confirmed the evolutionary conservation of Slc35g3 among vertebrates (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by TreeFam database analysis and referenced figure showing phylogenetic conservation.

claim: Slc35g3 expression begins 21 days postpartum in mice.
source: RT-PCR analysis indicates that it is prominently expressed in the testis, beginning 21 days postpartum (Figure 1B), suggesting that its expression begins in round spermatids in mice.
evidence: RT-PCR experimental data showing temporal expression pattern.

claim: Slc35g3 expression begins in round spermatids in mice.
source: RT-PCR analysis indicates that it is prominently expressed in the testis, beginning 21 days postpartum (Figure 1B), suggesting that its expression begins in round spermatids in mice.
evidence: Inference based on RT-PCR timing data and knowledge of spermatogenesis stages.

claim: Slc35g3 is the only mouse SLC35 family member that shows a testis-specific transcription pattern.
source: The Mammalian Reproductive Genetics Database (Robertson et al., 2020) revealed that Slc35g3 is the only mouse SLC35 family that shows a testis-specific transcription pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Database analysis showing unique expression pattern among SLC35 family members.

claim: Transcription of Slc35g3 initiates in round spermatids.
source: A previous scRNA-seq analysis suggested that transcription of Slc35g3 initiates in round spermatids (Figure 1C; Mouse Cell Atlas; 17).
evidence: Single-cell RNA sequencing data from Mouse Cell Atlas.

claim: SLC35G3 has 10 transmembrane domains.
source: Both AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) and TOPCONS (Tsirigos et al., 2015) analyses supported that SLC35G3 has 10 transmembrane domains (Figure 1D), likely forming a homodimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational structure prediction using AlphaFold2 and TOPCONS.

claim: SLC35G3 likely forms a homodimer.
source: Both AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) and TOPCONS (Tsirigos et al., 2015) analyses supported that SLC35G3 has 10 transmembrane domains (Figure 1D), likely forming a homodimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational structure prediction suggesting homodimeric arrangement.

claim: SLC35G3 colocalizes with Golgi marker GM130 in mouse testicular germ cells.
source: Immunostaining colocalizes SLC35G3 with Golgi marker (GM) 130 (Golgin A2), indicating SLC35G3 localization in the Golgi of mouse testicular germ cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Immunostaining experimental data showing colocalization.

claim: SLC35G3 is localized in the Golgi of mouse testicular germ cells.
source: Immunostaining colocalizes SLC35G3 with Golgi marker (GM) 130 (Golgin A2), indicating SLC35G3 localization in the Golgi of mouse testicular germ cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Immunostaining data showing colocalization with Golgi marker.

claim: Slc35g3 knockout mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 with an 1804 bp deletion on a hybrid B6D2 background.
source: To investigate the roles of Slc35g3 in male reproduction, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate a homozygous knockout mouse line (Slc35g3-/-) with an 1804 bp deletion on a hybrid B6D2 background.
evidence: Description of experimental method used to generate knockout mice.

claim: The 1804 bp deletion in Slc35g3 knockout mice resulted in the loss of the entire Slc35g3 coding region.
source: This deletion resulted in the loss of the entire Slc35g3 coding region (Figure 2A and B), indicating that it should be a null allele.
evidence: Molecular characterization of the deletion showing complete loss of coding sequence.

claim: The Slc35g3 deletion is a null allele.
source: This deletion resulted in the loss of the entire Slc35g3 coding region (Figure 2A and B), indicating that it should be a null allele.
evidence: Inference based on complete loss of coding region.

claim: Slc35g3-/- mice exhibit grossly normal development, appearance, and behavior.
source: Slc35g3-/- mice exhibit grossly normal development, appearance, and behavior, consistent with its testis-restricted expression.
evidence: Observational data on knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: Absence of Slc35g3 mRNA in Slc35g3-/- testes was verified by RNA-seq.
source: Absence of the Slc35g3 mRNA and SLC35G3 protein in the Slc35g3-/- testes was verified by RNA-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and western blot analysis (Figure 2C), respectively.
evidence: RNA-seq data confirming absence of transcript.

claim: Absence of SLC35G3 protein in Slc35g3-/- testes was verified by western blot analysis.
source: Absence of the Slc35g3 mRNA and SLC35G3 protein in the Slc35g3-/- testes was verified by RNA-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and western blot analysis (Figure 2C), respectively.
evidence: Western blot data confirming absence of protein.

claim: SLC35G3 is expressed in the testis but not in epididymal sperm.
source: The specific expression of SLC35G3 in the testis, but not in epididymal sperm, suggests that its function is restricted to spermatogenesis.
evidence: Expression pattern data from western blot analysis.

claim: SLC35G3 function is restricted to spermatogenesis.
source: The specific expression of SLC35G3 in the testis, but not in epididymal sperm, suggests that its function is restricted to spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inference based on expression pattern limited to testis.

claim: SLC35G3 is absent in the Golgi of Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: Moreover, immunofluorescence of SLC35G3 confirmed its absence in the Golgi of Slc35g3-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing absence of protein in knockout.

claim: Testes of Slc35g3-/- male mice appeared normal in both appearance and weight.
source: Testes of Slc35g3-/- male mice appeared normal in both appearance and weight (Figure 2D and E; +/+ vs. -/-, two-sided Student's t-test; p=0.42).
evidence: Morphological and weight measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Slc35g3-/- male mice are sterile.
source: Despite successful copulation, as evidenced by the presence of vaginal plugs, Slc35g3-/- male mice are sterile (Figure 2F; +/+vs. -/-, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=2.87 × 10–10).
evidence: Fertility testing data showing complete sterility with statistical significance.

claim: Slc35g3-/- male mice successfully copulate as evidenced by the presence of vaginal plugs.
source: Despite successful copulation, as evidenced by the presence of vaginal plugs, Slc35g3-/- male mice are sterile (Figure 2F; +/+vs. -/-, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=2.87 × 10–10).
evidence: Observational data from mating experiments.

claim: Examination of seminiferous tubule and epididymis sections revealed no overt abnormalities in Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: Examination of seminiferous tubule and epididymis sections revealed no overt abnormalities (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Histological analysis showing normal tissue structure.

claim: Computer-assisted sperm analysis revealed no significant differences in the motility of sperm from control and Slc35g3-/- males.
source: Furthermore, computer-assisted sperm analysis revealed no significant differences in the motility of sperm from control and Slc35g3-/- males (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Quantitative sperm motility analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: Slc35g3-/--derived sperm could be differentiated from wild-type-derived sperm based on PC2 analysis of the tip of the sperm heads.
source: Wild-type-derived sperm and Slc35g3-/--derived sperm could be differentiated based on their PC2 analysis of the tip of the sperm heads, with Slc35g3-/--derived sperm displaying a relatively higher PC2 value (Figure 3C), indicating the lack of the hook shape in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Principal component analysis of sperm head morphology.

claim: Slc35g3-/--derived sperm display a relatively higher PC2 value.
source: Wild-type-derived sperm and Slc35g3-/--derived sperm could be differentiated based on their PC2 analysis of the tip of the sperm heads, with Slc35g3-/--derived sperm displaying a relatively higher PC2 value (Figure 3C), indicating the lack of the hook shape in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Quantitative morphological analysis data.

claim: Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lack the hook shape.
source: Wild-type-derived sperm and Slc35g3-/--derived sperm could be differentiated based on their PC2 analysis of the tip of the sperm heads, with Slc35g3-/--derived sperm displaying a relatively higher PC2 value (Figure 3C), indicating the lack of the hook shape in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Morphological analysis indicating altered sperm head shape.

claim: The head shape of Slc35g3-/--derived sperm resembled that of sperm from Fam71f2-/- mice.
source: The head shape of Slc35g3 -/--derived sperm resembled that of sperm from Fam71f2 -/- (recently renamed as Garin1a, Golgi-associated RAB2 interactor 1A) (Morohoshi et al., 2021) mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparative morphological analysis with another knockout model.

claim: Slc35g3-/- mice exhibited a more severe fertility phenotype compared to Fam71f2-/- mice.
source: However, Slc35g3-/- mice exhibited a more severe fertility phenotype compared to Fam71f2 -/- mice (average litter size = 0 and 4.4 pups/litter, respectively), suggesting that sperm head morphology is not the sole cause of sterility in Slc35g3-/- mice.
evidence: Comparative fertility data between two knockout models.

claim: Sperm head morphology is not the sole cause of sterility in Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: However, Slc35g3-/- mice exhibited a more severe fertility phenotype compared to Fam71f2 -/- mice (average litter size = 0 and 4.4 pups/litter, respectively), suggesting that sperm head morphology is not the sole cause of sterility in Slc35g3-/- mice.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of fertility phenotypes between models with similar head morphology.

claim: No oocytes were fertilized with spermatozoa from Slc35g3-/- males in conventional IVF using cumulus-intact oocytes.
source: We first performed conventional IVF using cumulus-intact oocytes with 2×105 sperm/mL insemination and found no oocytes fertilized with spermatozoa from Slc35g3-/- males (Figure 4A).
evidence: In vitro fertilization experimental data.

claim: There is a decline in the number of Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa bound to the zona pellucida.
source: By removing cumulus cells followed by insemination (Figure 4B), we found a decline in the number of Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa bound to the ZP (Figure 4C and D), no oocytes fertilized as well (Figure 4E, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p=0.0079).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of sperm-ZP binding in IVF experiments.

claim: No oocytes were fertilized with Slc35g3-/--derived sperm in cumulus-free IVF.
source: By removing cumulus cells followed by insemination (Figure 4B), we found a decline in the number of Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa bound to the ZP (Figure 4C and D), no oocytes fertilized as well (Figure 4E, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p=0.0079).
evidence: IVF experimental data showing no fertilization.

claim: A significantly lower number of Slc35g3-/--derived sperm fuse with ZP-free oocytes compared to control.
source: Further study, using ZP-free oocytes preloaded with Hoechst33342 (Figure 4F), revealed a significantly lower number of sperm fusing with the oocyte compared to control Slc35g3+/- (Figure 4G and H, +/- vs. -/-, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=1.71 × 10–21).
evidence: Quantitative fusion assay data with statistical analysis.

claim: Oolemma fusion and fertilization were improved with a 10 times higher sperm concentration from Slc35g3-/- males but were still significantly decreased compared to lower concentrations of sperm from controls.
source: Notably, oolemma fusion and fertilization were improved with a 10 times higher sperm concentration from Slc35g3-/- males but were still significantly decreased compared to the lower concentrations of sperm from controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Dose-response IVF experimental data.

claim: IVF using cumulus-intact oocytes with 10 times more sperm insemination resulted in a reduced fertilization rate of 45.7% (21/46) for Slc35g3-/- sperm.
source: Lastly, IVF performed using cumulus-intact oocytes with 10 times more sperm insemination (2×106 sperm/mL) resulted in a reduced fertilization rate (45.7%, 21/46), but we succeeded in obtaining 10 live pups from these fertilized eggs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: IVF experimental data with high sperm concentration.

claim: 10 live pups were obtained from fertilized eggs produced by IVF with high concentration Slc35g3-/- sperm.
source: Lastly, IVF performed using cumulus-intact oocytes with 10 times more sperm insemination (2×106 sperm/mL) resulted in a reduced fertilization rate (45.7%, 21/46), but we succeeded in obtaining 10 live pups from these fertilized eggs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Embryo transfer experimental data showing viable offspring.

claim: Slc35g3-/--derived sperm have defects in zona pellucida binding and oolemma fusion ability but produce viable offspring.
source: Our results indicate that Slc35g3-/--derived sperm have defects in ZP binding and oolemma fusion ability but produce viable offspring.
evidence: Summary of IVF experimental results.

claim: Control Slc35g3+/--derived sperm were observed within the oviduct two hours after copulation.
source: Two hours after copulation with wild-type female mice (Figure 5B), control Slc35g3+/--derived sperm tail signals marked by red fluorescence were observed within the oviduct (Figure 5C).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data from sperm migration assay.

claim: Slc35g3-/--derived sperm were found in the uterus but not in the oviduct.
source: In contrast, Slc35g3-/--derived sperm were found in the uterus but not in the oviduct (Figure 5C).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy data from sperm migration assay.

claim: Defective uterotubal junction migration is one of the primary causes of Slc35g3-/- male infertility.
source: Thus, the defective UTJ migration is one of the primary causes of Slc35g3-/- male infertility.
evidence: Inference based on sperm migration assay results.

claim: Immunoblot analysis showed a reduction in the amount of ZPBP1 in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates.
source: Immunoblot analysis of Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testis lysates showed a reduction in the amount of ZP binding protein 1 (ZPBP1; Lin et al., 2007), whereas Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif containing (GOPC; Yao et al., 2002) levels remained unchanged (Figure 6A).
evidence: Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: GOPC levels remained unchanged in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates.
source: Immunoblot analysis of Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testis lysates showed a reduction in the amount of ZP binding protein 1 (ZPBP1; Lin et al., 2007), whereas Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif containing (GOPC; Yao et al., 2002) levels remained unchanged (Figure 6A).
evidence: Western blot data showing unchanged protein levels.

claim: SPACA1 exhibited a subtle difference in banding pattern in the Slc35g3-/- testis lysate.
source: Interestingly, SPACA1 (Sperm Acrosome Associated 1; Fujihara et al., 2012) exhibited a subtle difference in banding pattern in the Slc35g3-/- testis lysate.
evidence: Western blot observation of altered protein migration pattern.

claim: SPACA1 is N-glycosylated.
source: SPACA1 is N-glycosylated, and treatment of testis and caudal sperm lysates with peptide-N-glycosidase F (PNGase F; Figure 6B and C) resulted in comparable SPACA1 band patterns between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testes but not in sperm lysates.
evidence: Known property of SPACA1 protein.

claim: Treatment with PNGase F resulted in comparable SPACA1 band patterns between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testes but not in sperm lysates.
source: SPACA1 is N-glycosylated, and treatment of testis and caudal sperm lysates with peptide-N-glycosidase F (PNGase F; Figure 6B and C) resulted in comparable SPACA1 band patterns between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testes but not in sperm lysates.
evidence: Enzymatic deglycosylation experiment showing differential effects in testis vs sperm.

claim: A similar result for SPACA1 was reported in Fam71f1-/- mice.
source: A similar result was also reported in Fam71f1 -/- (Garin1b; Morohoshi et al., 2021) mice, which exhibit abnormal acrosome formation.
evidence: Reference to published findings in another knockout model.

claim: Levels of ADAM1B were comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in the testis and sperm.
source: Levels of a disintegrin and metalloprotease (ADAM) 1B (Kim et al., 2006) were comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in the testis (Figure 6D) and sperm (Figure 6E).
evidence: Western blot data showing no change in protein levels.

claim: Levels of CMTM2A and CMTM2B were reduced in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates but not in sperm.
source: Levels of CKLF-like MARVEL transmembrane domain containing (CMTM) 2A and CMTM2B (Fujihara et al., 2018b) were reduced in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates but not in sperm.
evidence: Western blot data showing tissue-specific protein reduction.

claim: The expression pattern of ADAM3 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testis.
source: The expression pattern of ADAM3 (Shamsadin et al., 1999; Yamaguchi et al., 2009) was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testis, yet the amount of a smaller isoform was elevated in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates, indicating aberrant processing.
evidence: Western blot data showing similar testis expression.

claim: The amount of a smaller ADAM3 isoform was elevated in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates, indicating aberrant processing.
source: The expression pattern of ADAM3 (Shamsadin et al., 1999; Yamaguchi et al., 2009) was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testis, yet the amount of a smaller isoform was elevated in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates, indicating aberrant processing.
evidence: Western blot data showing altered protein processing.

claim: After PNGaseF treatment, the ADAM3 band pattern was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/-.
source: After PNGaseF treatment of proteins, the ADAM3 band pattern was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Enzymatic deglycosylation experiment showing glycosylation-dependent differences.

claim: The amount of TEX101 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testis lysates.
source: Given the aberrant ADAM3 band pattern was also observed in testis expressed gene 101 (TEX101) knockout (Fujihara et al., 2013) epididymal caput sperm, we examined TEX101 levels through western blot analysis; however, the amount of TEX101 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testis lysates (Figure 6D).
evidence: Western blot data showing no change in protein levels.

claim: The amount of t-ACE was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in both testis and sperm lysates.
source: Given that the testicular Ace-/- (t-ACE; Krege et al., 1995, Hagaman et al., 1998, Yamaguchi et al., 2006) caused aberrant localization of ADAM3, we examined t-ACE levels through western blot analysis and found that the amount of t-ACE was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in both testis and sperm lysates (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Western blot data showing no change in protein levels.

claim: The amount of LY6K was reduced in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates.
source: The amount of LY6K was reduced in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates (Figure 6D), and the amount of SPACA4 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in both testis and sperm lysates (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: The amount of SPACA4 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in both testis and sperm lysates.
source: The amount of LY6K was reduced in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates (Figure 6D), and the amount of SPACA4 was comparable between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- in both testis and sperm lysates (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Western blot data showing no change in protein levels.

claim: The amount of LYPD4 in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates decreased.
source: However, the amount of LYPD4 in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates decreased, and the lower molecular weight band disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates (Figure 6E), indicating the occurrence of a protein processing error or another non-N-linked oligosaccharide post-translational defect.
evidence: Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: The lower molecular weight band of LYPD4 disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates.
source: However, the amount of LYPD4 in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates decreased, and the lower molecular weight band disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates (Figure 6E), indicating the occurrence of a protein processing error or another non-N-linked oligosaccharide post-translational defect.
evidence: Western blot data showing altered protein processing.

claim: The disappearance of the lower molecular weight LYPD4 band indicates the occurrence of a protein processing error or another non-N-linked oligosaccharide post-translational defect.
source: However, the amount of LYPD4 in Slc35g3-/- testis lysates decreased, and the lower molecular weight band disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm lysates (Figure 6E), indicating the occurrence of a protein processing error or another non-N-linked oligosaccharide post-translational defect.
evidence: Inference based on altered protein migration pattern.

claim: IZUMO1 is an N-glycosylated acrosome membrane protein essential for sperm-oolemma fusion.
source: IZUMO1 is an N-glycosylated acrosome membrane protein, and the first to be identified as essential for sperm-oolemma fusion using knockout mice (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: Reference to established knowledge about IZUMO1 function.

claim: The levels of IZUMO1 decreased in both the testis and sperm of Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: The levels of IZUMO1 decreased in both the testis and sperm of Slc35g3-/- mice.
evidence: Western blot data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: IZUMO1 could relocate to the equatorial segment where fusion occurs after the acrosome reaction in Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa.
source: Although the amount of IZUMO1 in sperm was less, we did not see any other bands in the western blot analysis. IZUMO1 could relocate to the equatorial segment where fusion occurs after the acrosome reaction in Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing protein localization after acrosome reaction.

claim: EQTN is an O-linked glycosylated protein on the inner acrosomal membrane.
source: Equatorin (EQTN) is an O-linked glycosylated protein on the inner acrosomal membrane, not essential for oolemma fusion but rather functions in oolemma binding.
evidence: Known property of EQTN protein.

claim: EQTN is not essential for oolemma fusion but rather functions in oolemma binding.
source: Equatorin (EQTN) is an O-linked glycosylated protein on the inner acrosomal membrane, not essential for oolemma fusion but rather functions in oolemma binding.
evidence: Known functional property of EQTN.

claim: The EQTN signal showed no difference between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testes.
source: The EQTN signal showed no difference between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testes, but it disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Western blot data showing similar testis expression.

claim: The EQTN signal disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
source: The EQTN signal showed no difference between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- testes, but it disappeared in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Western blot data showing loss of antibody recognition in sperm.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of sperm lysates showed comparable quantitative values of EQTN between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: Intriguingly, mass spectrometry analysis of sperm lysates showed comparable quantitative values of EQTN between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/- mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data showing similar protein abundance.

claim: The anti-EQTN antibody MN9 recognizes both peptide and glycan structures.
source: With the fact that the anti-EQTN antibody MN9 recognizes both peptide and glycan structures and that the glycan structure (Toshimori et al., 1992), our data suggests that EQTN glycosylation is aberrant in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Known property of the antibody used.

claim: EQTN glycosylation is aberrant in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
source: With the fact that the anti-EQTN antibody MN9 recognizes both peptide and glycan structures and that the glycan structure (Toshimori et al., 1992), our data suggests that EQTN glycosylation is aberrant in Slc35g3-/--derived sperm.
evidence: Inference based on discrepancy between western blot and mass spectrometry data combined with antibody specificity.

claim: No difference was seen in the intensity and band pattern of SPACA6 using western blot analysis between Slc35g3+/- and Slc35g3-/-.
source: SPACA6 is known to be lost from all the sperm-oolemma fusion defective sperm (i.e., Dcst1/2, Fimp, Izumo1, Sof1, Spaca6, and Tmem95 knockout models) (Noda et al., 2020); however, we did not see any difference in the intensity and band pattern using western blot analysis.
evidence: Western blot data showing no change in protein levels or processing.

claim: The band patterns of ConA, AAL, and MAL-II were comparable between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- testis samples.
source: The band patterns of concanavalin A (ConA; detecting mannose), Aleuria aurantia lectin (AAL; detecting fucose), and Maackia amurensis II (MAL-II; detecting sialic acid +core1 structure) were comparable between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- samples.
evidence: Lectin blot data showing similar glycan patterns.

claim: With PNA lectin, the intensity of a band around 60 kDa increased in Slc35g3-/- testis.
source: Notably, with PNA, which detects galactose β1–3 acetyl galactosamine (core 1 structure), the intensity of a band around 60 kDa increased in Slc35g3-/- testis.
evidence: Lectin blot data showing increased signal intensity.

claim: PNA binding is inhibited by any galactose modifications.
source: As PNA binding is known to be inhibited by any galactose modifications (Bojar et al., 2022), the core 1 modifications might be disrupted in the target protein.
evidence: Known property of PNA lectin binding.

claim: The core 1 modifications might be disrupted in the target protein in Slc35g3-/- testis.
source: As PNA binding is known to be inhibited by any galactose modifications (Bojar et al., 2022), the core 1 modifications might be disrupted in the target protein.
evidence: Inference based on increased PNA binding and known lectin specificity.

claim: With LSL-N lectin, signal intensities for small proteins decreased in Slc35g3-/- testis.
source: With Laetiporus sulphureus lectin N-terminal domain (LSL-N; detecting LacNAc: galactose-GlcNAc), signal intensities for small proteins decreased.
evidence: Lectin blot data showing decreased signal intensity.

claim: Some major signals disappeared in PNA and LSL-N blot analysis of mature spermatozoa from Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: Intriguingly, the difference became evident when we performed lectin blot analysis using mature spermatozoa. Some major signals disappeared in PNA and LSL-N blot analysis (Figure 7B).
evidence: Lectin blot data showing loss of signals in sperm.

claim: The introduction of Slc35b2 did not rescue the amounts of proteins with GlcNAc modification in SLC35B4 knockout cells.
source: We found that the introduction of Slc35b2 did not rescue the amounts of proteins with GlcNAc modification (Figure 7C).
evidence: Lectin blot data from rescue experiment in cell culture.

claim: Transfection with the Slc35b4-expressing plasmid rescued GlcNAc modification levels in SLC35B4 knockout cells.
source: Conversely, transfection with the Slc35b4-expressing plasmid rescued GlcNAc modification levels.
evidence: Lectin blot data from rescue experiment in cell culture.

claim: LSL-N signals were rescued by Slc35g3 transfection in SLC35B4 knockout cells.
source: Further, the LSL-N signals were rescued by Slc35g3 transfection (Figure 7C), suggesting that SLC35G3 functions as a UDP-GlcNAc transporter.
evidence: Lectin blot data from rescue experiment in cell culture.

claim: SLC35G3 functions as a UDP-GlcNAc transporter.
source: Further, the LSL-N signals were rescued by Slc35g3 transfection (Figure 7C), suggesting that SLC35G3 functions as a UDP-GlcNAc transporter.
evidence: Inference based on rescue of GlcNAc-dependent glycosylation in cell culture.

claim: The T179HfsTer27 frame mutation has a relatively high allele frequency (1.88e–3) in human genomes.
source: Among the frameshift mutations found in human genomes (n=76156,, gnomAD; 42), the T179HfsTer27 frame mutation has a relatively high allele frequency (1.88e–3), and homozygous mutations are observed in 54 individuals (29 females and 25 males).
evidence: Population genetics data from gnomAD database.

claim: Homozygous T179HfsTer27 mutations are observed in 54 individuals (29 females and 25 males).
source: Among the frameshift mutations found in human genomes (n=76156,, gnomAD; 42), the T179HfsTer27 frame mutation has a relatively high allele frequency (1.88e–3), and homozygous mutations are observed in 54 individuals (29 females and 25 males).
evidence: Population genetics data from gnomAD database.

claim: AlphaMissense predicted 35 pathogenic missense mutations in the SLC35G3 gene.
source: Moreover, AlphaMissense (Cheng et al., 2023), a deep learning model trained on protein sequences and annotations of pathogenicity, predicted 35 pathogenic missense mutations in the SLC35G3 gene.
evidence: Computational prediction using AlphaMissense tool.

claim: Two mutations (F215L and F267L) were identified in human genomes among the predicted pathogenic mutations.
source: Among these, two mutations (F215L and F267L) were identified in human genomes, and we focused on F267L, which showed potential detrimental effects according to the evolutionary conservation and protein 3D structure (PolyPhen-2; 44).
evidence: Identification of mutations in human genome databases.

claim: F267L showed potential detrimental effects according to evolutionary conservation and protein 3D structure.
source: Among these, two mutations (F215L and F267L) were identified in human genomes, and we focused on F267L, which showed potential detrimental effects according to the evolutionary conservation and protein 3D structure (PolyPhen-2; 44).
evidence: Computational prediction using PolyPhen-2 tool.

claim: The signal decreased by SLC35B4-/- was rescued by the introduction of wild-type SLC35G3.
source: With lectin blot analysis using LSL-N, the signal decreased by SLC35B4-/- was rescued by the introduction of wild-type SLC35G3, while no signal recovery was observed upon the introduction of FS or F267L (Figure 7D).
evidence: Lectin blot data from rescue experiment with wild-type protein.

claim: No signal recovery was observed upon the introduction of T179HfsTer27 or F267L mutants in SLC35B4-/- cells.
source: With lectin blot analysis using LSL-N, the signal decreased by SLC35B4-/- was rescued by the introduction of wild-type SLC35G3, while no signal recovery was observed upon the introduction of FS or F267L (Figure 7D).
evidence: Lectin blot data from rescue experiment with mutant proteins.

claim: The T179HfsTer27 and F267L mutations result in loss of function.
source: These findings suggest a loss of function in the T179HfsTer27 and F267L mutations.
evidence: Inference based on failure to rescue glycosylation defect in cell culture.

claim: Mouse SLC35G3 has UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity.
source: Mouse SLC35G3 has UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity, and its ablation caused abnormal processing of the sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane proteins.
evidence: Summary of functional characterization from rescue experiments.

claim: Ablation of SLC35G3 caused abnormal processing of the sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane proteins.
source: Mouse SLC35G3 has UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity, and its ablation caused abnormal processing of the sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane proteins.
evidence: Summary of protein analysis findings in knockout mice.

claim: Reported human SLC35G3 mutations (F267L and T179HfsTer27) diminished the UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity of SLC35G3.
source: Reported human SLC35G3 mutations (F267L and T179HfsTer27) diminished the UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity of SLC35G3, implying infertility risks in males carrying these mutations.
evidence: Functional assay data showing loss of transporter activity.

claim: Human SLC35G3 mutations (F267L and T179HfsTer27) imply infertility risks in males carrying these mutations.
source: Reported human SLC35G3 mutations (F267L and T179HfsTer27) diminished the UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity of SLC35G3, implying infertility risks in males carrying these mutations.
evidence: Inference based on loss of function in vitro and mouse knockout phenotype.

claim: Slc35g3 emerged in amphibians and is conserved in primates.
source: Slc35g3 emerged in amphibians and is conserved in primates.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis showing evolutionary origin and conservation.

claim: SLC35G3 is a spermatogenic cell-specific UDP-GlcNAc transporter.
source: We discovered that SLC35G3 is a spermatogenic cell-specific UDP-GlcNAc transporter, and Slc35g3 ablation results in abnormal processing of sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane glycoproteins required for sperm-fertilizing ability and male fertility.
evidence: Summary of expression pattern and functional characterization.

claim: Slc35g3 ablation results in abnormal processing of sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane glycoproteins required for sperm-fertilizing ability and male fertility.
source: We discovered that SLC35G3 is a spermatogenic cell-specific UDP-GlcNAc transporter, and Slc35g3 ablation results in abnormal processing of sperm plasma membrane and acrosome membrane glycoproteins required for sperm-fertilizing ability and male fertility.
evidence: Summary of protein analysis and fertility phenotype findings.

claim: Slc35g3 knockout male mice were sterile due to impaired sperm functions in uterotubal junction passage, zona pellucida binding, and oocyte fusion.
source: In this study, we found that Slc35g3 knockout male mice were sterile due to impaired sperm functions in uterotubal junction passage, zona pellucida binding, and oocyte fusion.
evidence: Summary of multiple functional assays showing sperm defects.

claim: Glycosylation is a post-translational modification that ensures target protein synthesis, secretion, stability, characterization, and/or function.
source: Glycosylation is a post-translational modification that ensures target protein synthesis, secretion, stability, characterization, and/or function (Matzuk and Boime, 1988; Matzuk et al., 1989; Schjoldager et al., 2020).
evidence: Established knowledge about glycosylation supported by citations.

claim: In the endoplasmic reticulum, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex co-translationally transfers core glycans assembled on dolichol phosphate to asparagine residues of nascent proteins.
source: In the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the oligosaccharyltransferase complex (OSTC) co-translationally transfers core glycans assembled on dolichol phosphate to asparagine residues of nascent proteins.
evidence: Established knowledge about N-glycosylation pathway.

claim: FREY tightly interacts with proteins involved in N-glycosylation, and its disruption destabilizes OSTC and causes subsequent ablation of the acrosomal membrane proteins essential for sperm-egg fusion.
source: Recent studies suggest that FREY tightly interacts with proteins involved in N-glycosylation, and its disruption destabilizes OSTC and causes subsequent ablation of the acrosomal membrane proteins essential for sperm-egg fusion (Contreras et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2023).
evidence: Summary of recent published findings.

claim: Testis-specific paralogs CLGN/CALR3/PDILT are required for ADAM3 sperm membrane glycoprotein maturation to equip sperm with fertilization competence, including the ability to pass through the uterotubal junction.
source: In addition to the CANX/CALR/PDI complex in somatic cells, their testis-specific paralogs, CLGN/CALR3/PDILT, are required for ADAM3 sperm membrane glycoprotein maturation to equip sperm with fertilization competence, including the ability to pass through the uterotubal junction (UTJ) (Tokuhiro et al., 2012).
evidence: Summary of published findings on testis-specific chaperones.

claim: Dpy19l2 knockout mice are infertile due to globozoospermia.
source: Dpy19l2 knockout mice are infertile due to globozoospermia (Pierre et al., 2012), and a mutation in Galntl5 resulted in asthenozoospermia (Takasaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of published knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: A mutation in Galntl5 resulted in asthenozoospermia.
source: Dpy19l2 knockout mice are infertile due to globozoospermia (Pierre et al., 2012), and a mutation in Galntl5 resulted in asthenozoospermia (Takasaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of published mutation phenotype.

claim: GALNTL5 does not exhibit transferase activity in vitro.
source: Of note, GALNTL5 does not exhibit transferase activity in vitro (Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of published biochemical characterization.

claim: Mgat4d knockout mice are fertile.
source: While Mgat4d knockout mice are fertile (Raman et al., 2012), Mgat4e and Mgat4f orthologs do not exist in humans, and their knockout mice need to be generated to reveal if they have indispensable or redundant functions in mice.
evidence: Summary of published knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: Mgat4e and Mgat4f orthologs do not exist in humans.
source: While Mgat4d knockout mice are fertile (Raman et al., 2012), Mgat4e and Mgat4f orthologs do not exist in humans, and their knockout mice need to be generated to reveal if they have indispensable or redundant functions in mice.
evidence: Statement about gene orthology between species.

claim: Spermatogenic cells have a unique system for the production and quality control of glycoproteins, and some of them are critical for spermatogenesis, sperm functions, and male fertility.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the spermatogenic cells have a unique system for the production and quality control of glycoproteins, and some of them are critical for spermatogenesis, sperm functions, and male fertility.
evidence: Inference based on multiple cited studies showing testis-specific glycosylation machinery.

claim: SLC35 family members are nucleotide sugar transporters responsible for importing sugars that serve as substrates for glycosyltransferases.
source: In the present study, we focused on the solute carrier (SLC) 35 family of nucleotide sugar transporters, which are responsible for importing sugars that serve as substrates for glycosyltransferases.
evidence: Established knowledge about SLC35 family function.

claim: SLC35A1 transports CMP-Sialic Acid.
source: Among the SLC35 paralogs, SLC35A1 transports CMP-Sialic Acid, SLC35A2 transports UDP-Gal, SLC35B4 transports UDP-GlcNAc, and SLC35C1 transports GDP-Fuc (Ahuja and Whorton, 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge about specific transporter substrates.

claim: SLC35A2 transports UDP-Gal.
source: Among the SLC35 paralogs, SLC35A1 transports CMP-Sialic Acid, SLC35A2 transports UDP-Gal, SLC35B4 transports UDP-GlcNAc, and SLC35C1 transports GDP-Fuc (Ahuja and Whorton, 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge about specific transporter substrates.

claim: SLC35B4 transports UDP-GlcNAc.
source: Among the SLC35 paralogs, SLC35A1 transports CMP-Sialic Acid, SLC35A2 transports UDP-Gal, SLC35B4 transports UDP-GlcNAc, and SLC35C1 transports GDP-Fuc (Ahuja and Whorton, 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge about specific transporter substrates.

claim: SLC35C1 transports GDP-Fuc.
source: Among the SLC35 paralogs, SLC35A1 transports CMP-Sialic Acid, SLC35A2 transports UDP-Gal, SLC35B4 transports UDP-GlcNAc, and SLC35C1 transports GDP-Fuc (Ahuja and Whorton, 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge about specific transporter substrates.

claim: Most SLC35 family members show ubiquitous expressions, including in spermatogenic cells.
source: Of the 27 SLC35 family members, most show ubiquitous expressions, including in spermatogenic cells.
evidence: Statement about expression patterns of SLC35 family.

claim: During spermatogenesis, Slc35b4 is expressed in earlier stages, but it decreases and is replaced by Slc35g3 in later stages.
source: During spermatogenesis, Slc35b4 is expressed in earlier stages, but it decreases and is replaced by Slc35g3 in later stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Expression pattern analysis showing temporal regulation.

claim: The reason for the stage-dependent usage of two transporters is unknown.
source: The reason for the stage-dependent usage of two transporters is unknown, but it may be related to the formation of acrosomes, which are rich in glycosylated proteins, in the later stages of spermatogenesis.
evidence: Acknowledgment of unknown mechanism.

claim: The stage-dependent usage of two transporters may be related to the formation of acrosomes, which are rich in glycosylated proteins, in the later stages of spermatogenesis.
source: The reason for the stage-dependent usage of two transporters is unknown, but it may be related to the formation of acrosomes, which are rich in glycosylated proteins, in the later stages of spermatogenesis.
evidence: Speculation about biological rationale for expression pattern.

claim: SLC35B4 and SLC35G3 may have different activities and/or functions.
source: Although our in vitro data showed no clear differences (Figure 7C), SLC35B4 and SLC35G3 may have different activities and/or functions.
evidence: Speculation about potential functional differences despite similar in vitro activity.

claim: SLC35G3 may have a lower optimal temperature because spermatogenesis progresses at a lower temperature.
source: Alternatively, SLC35G3 may have a lower optimal temperature because spermatogenesis progresses at a lower temperature (Bedford, 1991).
evidence: Speculation about temperature adaptation based on known biology of spermatogenesis.

claim: The transcript level of Slc35g3 in later spermatogenesis stages (highest TPM = 320 at round spermatid) is higher than that of Slc35b4 in the earlier stage (highest TPM = 21 at spermatogonia).
source: Considering the transcript level of Slc35g3 in later spermatogenesis stages (highest TPM = 320 at round spermatid) is higher than that of Slc35b4 in the earlier stage (highest TPM = 21 at spermatogonia), spermatids may simply require more UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity.
evidence: Quantitative expression data from transcriptomics.

claim: Spermatids may simply require more UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity.
source: Considering the transcript level of Slc35g3 in later spermatogenesis stages (highest TPM = 320 at round spermatid) is higher than that of Slc35b4 in the earlier stage (highest TPM = 21 at spermatogonia), spermatids may simply require more UDP-GlcNAc transporter activity.
evidence: Inference based on higher expression levels in later stages.

claim: Lectin blot analyses revealed no differences in ConA signals targeting terminal mannose between Slc35g3+/+ and Slc35g3-/- samples.
source: Lectin blot analyses revealed no differences in ConA signals targeting terminal mannose (Figure 7B), indicating the normal formation of high-mannose-type oligosaccharides for N-glycan biosynthesis in the ER of Slc35g3-/- spermatogenic cells (Aebi, 2013).
evidence: Lectin blot data showing no change in mannose-containing glycans.

claim: Normal formation of high-mannose-type oligosaccharides for N-glycan biosynthesis occurs in the ER of Slc35g3-/- spermatogenic cells.
source: Lectin blot analyses revealed no differences in ConA signals targeting terminal mannose (Figure 7B), indicating the normal formation of high-mannose-type oligosaccharides for N-glycan biosynthesis in the ER of Slc35g3-/- spermatogenic cells (Aebi, 2013).
evidence: Inference based on normal ConA lectin binding pattern.

claim: SLC35G3 plays a more important role in glycan elongation rather than core structure.
source: These findings suggest that SLC35G3 plays a more important role in glycan elongation rather than core structure, and the impaired elongated glycan structure affected the properties of glycoproteins and following sperm morphology and functions in Slc35g3-/- mice.
evidence: Inference based on lectin blot patterns showing normal core structures but altered elongated structures.

claim: The impaired elongated glycan structure affected the properties of glycoproteins and following sperm morphology and functions in Slc35g3-/- mice.
source: These findings suggest that SLC35G3 plays a more important role in glycan elongation rather than core structure, and the impaired elongated glycan structure affected the properties of glycoproteins and following sperm morphology and functions in Slc35g3-/- mice.
evidence: Inference connecting glycosylation defects to observed phenotypes.

claim: While spermatogenesis looked grossly normal in Slc35g3-/- mice, their spermatozoa displayed multiple phenotypic abnormalities in head morphology, UTJ migration, and fertilization.
source: While spermatogenesis looked grossly normal in Slc35g3-/- mice (Figure 2D, E and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), their spermatozoa displayed multiple phenotypic abnormalities in head morphology (Figure 3), UTJ migration (Figure 5), and fertilization (Figure 4).
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental findings showing normal spermatogenesis but abnormal sperm function.

claim: Most knockout mice with only subtle head malformation can produce offspring, although at lower levels.
source: Regarding sperm head malformation, while globozoospermia results in male infertility (e.g., Zpbp1 [Lin et al., 2007], Gopc [Yao et al., 2002], and Spaca1 [Fujihara et al., 2012] knockout mice), most of the knockout mice with only subtle head malformation can produce offspring, although at lower levels (e.g., Zpbp2 [Lin et al., 2007], Fam71f2 [Morohoshi et al., 2021], and Garin2-Garin5 [Wang et al., 2024] knockout mice).
evidence: Summary of published phenotypes from multiple knockout models.

claim: Mutations in multiple genes synergistically worsen head morphology, even in the heterozygous state.
source: For example, it has been shown that mutations in multiple genes synergistically worsen head morphology, even in the heterozygous state (Martinez et al., 2022).
evidence: Summary of published findings on genetic interactions.

claim: SLC35G3-mediated UDP-GlcNAc transport is important for ZPBP1 stabilization and SPACA1 processing.
source: Although we are still far from unraveling these molecular interactions, we have revealed the importance of SLC35G3-mediated UDP-GlcNAc transport for ZPBP1 stabilization and SPACA1 processing.
evidence: Summary of protein analysis findings showing effects on specific proteins.

claim: ADAM3 is absent from most knockout spermatozoa that exhibit defective UTJ passage and ZP binding.
source: These defects are commonly linked and observed in many infertile knockout mice, and ADAM3 is absent from most of these knockout spermatozoa (Fujihara et al., 2019; Fujihara et al., 2018a).
evidence: Summary of published findings from multiple knockout models.

claim: ADAM3 is present in the Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa as in four other knockout mouse lines that show the same phenotype.
source: However, ADAM3 is present in the Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa as in four other knockout mouse lines that show the same phenotype (i.e., Ly6k, Pgap1, Spaca4, and Lypd4 knockout lines).
evidence: Western blot data showing ADAM3 presence and comparison to other models.

claim: ADAM3 may be dysfunctional in Slc35g3-/- sperm, or there may be an unknown factor responsible for UTJ passage and ZP binding.
source: These results suggest that ADAM3 may be dysfunctional in these mutant sperm, or that there may be an unknown factor responsible for UTJ passage and ZP binding.
evidence: Speculation based on presence of ADAM3 but defective function.

claim: ADAM3 is no longer active in humans.
source: Since ADAM3 is no longer active in humans, more attention needs to be paid to LYPD4 to understand the sperm-fertilizing ability.
evidence: Known evolutionary difference between mouse and human.

claim: More attention needs to be paid to LYPD4 to understand the sperm-fertilizing ability in humans.
source: Since ADAM3 is no longer active in humans, more attention needs to be paid to LYPD4 to understand the sperm-fertilizing ability.
evidence: Inference about research priorities based on species differences.

claim: The lack of glycosylation is accompanied by a decrease in IZUMO1 levels and a reduction in the number of pups.
source: While we did not see any differences in SPACA6 western blot analysis, we found a decrease in IZUMO1 in Slc35g3-/--derived spermatozoa, which is consistent with our previous study showing the lack of glycosylation accompanied by a decrease in IZUMO1 levels and a reduction in the number of pups (Inoue et al., 2008).
evidence: Reference to previous published findings.

claim: The observed/expected ratio of single-nucleotide variants causing loss of function in SLC35G3 was 0.53, suggesting the presence of selective pressure due to mutations.
source: In addition, the observed/expected ratio of single-nucleotide variants causing loss of function was 0.53, suggesting the presence of selective pressure due to mutations.
evidence: Population genetics metric indicating constraint on loss-of-function mutations.

claim: Assessment of sperm-fertilizing ability in individuals with SLC35G3 mutations would be beneficial to understanding glycosylated protein synthesis and functions in human spermatozoa.
source: Assessment of their sperm-fertilizing ability would be beneficial to understanding glycosylated protein synthesis and functions in human spermatozoa.
evidence: Proposal for future research direction.

claim: Healthy offspring were obtained by IVF with higher concentration sperm insemination from Slc35g3-/- males.
source: Even if the mutation caused male infertility, as we obtained healthy offspring by IVF with higher concentration sperm insemination, intracytoplasmic sperm injection might not be necessary for their treatment.
evidence: Experimental data showing successful IVF with high sperm concentration.

claim: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection might not be necessary for treatment of infertility caused by SLC35G3 mutations.
source: Even if the mutation caused male infertility, as we obtained healthy offspring by IVF with higher concentration sperm insemination, intracytoplasmic sperm injection might not be necessary for their treatment.
evidence: Inference about potential clinical implications based on IVF success.

claim: SLC35G3 functions as a testis-specific UDP-GlcNAc transporter during late spermatogenesis.
source: In conclusion, our research suggests that SLC35G3 functions as a testis-specific UDP-GlcNAc transporter during late spermatogenesis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Glycosylation-related genes specific to the testis play a crucial role in the synthesis, quality control, and function of glycoproteins on sperm, which are essential for male fertility through their interactions with eggs and the female reproductive system.
source: We reaffirmed that glycosylation-related genes specific to the testis play a crucial role in the synthesis, quality control, and function of glycoproteins on sperm, which are essential for male fertility through their interactions with eggs and the female reproductive system.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating current findings with broader context.

claim: Human SLC35G3 exhibits transporter activity.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that human SLC35G3 also exhibits transporter activity and proposed a loss-of-function mutation that may cause male infertility.
evidence: Functional assay data showing activity of human protein.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in human SLC35G3 may cause male infertility.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that human SLC35G3 also exhibits transporter activity and proposed a loss-of-function mutation that may cause male infertility.
evidence: Inference based on loss of function in vitro and mouse phenotype.

claim: Further research on SLC35G3 and sperm glycoprotein synthesis has the potential to contribute to understanding the causes of male infertility, developing treatments, and advancing contraceptive methods.
source: Further research on this gene and sperm glycoprotein synthesis has the potential to contribute to understanding the causes of male infertility, developing treatments, and advancing contraceptive methods.
evidence: Statement about potential future applications and research directions.
